title: Choco-Q: Commute Hamiltonian-based QAOA for Constrained Binary Optimization
problem: Existing QAOA approaches for constrained binary optimization based on penalty terms or cyclic Hamiltonian simulation fail to encode arbitrary linear constraints, yielding near-zero success rates (as low as 0.02%) and long end-to-end latency. Decomposing the resulting Hamiltonians into deployable quantum circuits has exponential time and memory complexity.
method: Choco-Q encodes constraints by selecting a driver Hamiltonian that commutes with the constraint operator (the commute Hamiltonian), exploiting the Heisenberg picture to guarantee that constraint expectation values remain invariant during quantum evolution, achieving 100% in-constraints rate. Three optimization passes reduce circuit complexity for NISQ deployment: (1) Hamiltonian serialization decomposes the global commute Hamiltonian into independent local sub-Hamiltonians (proven via Lemma 1 to preserve constraint satisfaction), reducing circuit depth from ~4000 to ~24; (2) equivalent decomposition converts each local commute Hamiltonian into control-phase gates and CX gates with linear O(n) time complexity and O(n) circuit depth (Lemma 2), replacing exponential Trotter-Suzuki decomposition; (3) variable elimination reduces the constraint matrix dimension by removing variables with the most non-zero solution entries, shrinking qubit count and circuit depth at the cost of additional classical measurements. Evaluation is conducted on IBMQ Fez (159-qubit Heron r2), Sherbrooke, and Osaka (127-qubit Eagle r3) platforms, plus a classical GPU simulator (A100).

title: Accurate Leakage Speculation for Quantum Error Correction
problem: Physical qubits in quantum error correction (QEC) can leak into higher energy states (e.g., |2>), corrupting syndrome measurements and spreading errors to neighboring qubits; detecting leakage on data qubits is especially hard because they are never directly measured during QEC cycles.
method: GLADIATOR frames leakage detection as a graph labeling problem. Offline, it constructs a code-aware error-propagation graph whose nodes are syndrome patterns and weighted directed edges represent transition probabilities under leakage vs. non-leakage errors, calibrated to device characterization data. Each node accumulates incoming leakage-edge weights (W_L) and non-leakage-edge weights (W_NL); nodes where W_L > W_NL by a threshold factor are labeled as leakage patterns and compiled into a lookup table. Online, a parity-adjacency generator extracts a 5-bit syndrome pattern per data qubit each QEC cycle and a combinational sequence checker (at most 10 LUTs per data qubit) classifies it in under 1 ns, triggering an LRC only for patterns flagged as leakage-dominated. GLADIATOR-D extends the design to a two-round sliding window of syndrome history for further accuracy. The method generalizes to surface codes, color codes, and qLDPC codes.

title: VoLUT: Efficient Volumetric streaming enhanced by LUT-based super-resolution
problem: 3D volumetric video streaming requires extremely high bandwidth; downsampling before transmission and upsampling via super-resolution at the receiver is needed, but existing 3D SR algorithms are too slow for real-time use on commodity mobile devices.
method: VoLUT has a two-stage SR pipeline. Stage 1 (dilated kNN interpolation): broader spatial context via dilated k-nearest neighbor search for initial upsampling; octree parallelism accelerates the kNN computation; neighbor relationships are reused across upsampling steps. Stage 2 (LUT refinement): coordinates of upsampled points are normalized to [0,1], quantized into b discrete bins per axis (bin=128 by default), and looked up in a precomputed 3D LUT that stores high-resolution position offsets (RF=4 receptive field, bin=128 yields 1.6GB LUT). The LUT is built offline from a trained NN model. MPC (Model Predictive Control)-based adaptive bitrate algorithm dynamically selects downsampling rate based on network conditions, streaming a continuous range of quality levels.

title: Training Ultra Long Context Language Model with Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer
problem: Training LLMs on extremely long sequences (1M+ tokens) requires memory far exceeding GPU capacity; existing Ulysses-style sequence parallelism is bottlenecked by PCIe transfer latency when offloading to host memory.
method: Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer (FPDT) extends DeepSpeed Ulysses with CPU memory offloading using a double-buffer design. The sequence is sliced into chunks (default 64K tokens). A pipeline overlaps PCIe host-to-device prefetch of the next chunk with GPU computation on the current chunk. A rank-ordinal scatter redistributes activations across GPUs. The vocabulary computation is also pipelined within the sequence chunk pipeline.

title: Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures
problem: Training and serving 671B-parameter MoE LLMs at scale exposes critical hardware bottlenecks: HBM memory capacity growing <50%/year versus >1000%/year model memory demand, FP8 Tensor Core accumulation precision limited to 13 mantissa bits (FP22) causing numerical instability in large-scale training, NVLink bandwidth halved in H800 vs H100 (400 vs 900 GB/s) constraining tensor parallelism, and all-to-all expert parallelism (EP) communication consuming up to 20 GPU SMs for control-plane operations.
method: The paper presents DeepSeek-V3's production architecture and infrastructure as a case study, covering: (1) Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) that compresses KV cache from 516 KB/token (LLaMA-3.1-405B) to 70 KB/token via low-rank KV projection; (2) DeepSeekMoE with Node-Limited Routing constraining expert token dispatch to at most 4 of 8 nodes to exploit the 4:1 NVLink/IB bandwidth ratio, reducing inter-node IB traffic; (3) FP8 mixed-precision training with tile-wise 1x128 activation quantization and block-wise 128x128 weight quantization using DeepGEMM, requiring workarounds for FP22 accumulation precision on Hopper; (4) DualPipe overlapping MLA and MoE computation with all-to-all EP dispatch/combine via InfiniBand GPUDirect Async (IBGDA); (5) a Multi-Plane Two-Layer Fat-Tree (MPFT) network replacing a standard three-layer fat-tree, using 8 independent IB planes per node to support up to 16,384 GPUs at the same cost-per-endpoint as a two-layer topology. Experimental data includes real cluster training throughput (272.8B tokens/day, MFU 43.7%), EP bandwidth (>40 GB/s per GPU), and network latency comparisons (IB at 2.8 us same-leaf vs RoCE at 3.6 us).
